blocks.robotComment: A language that catches memory bugs before your program ever runs — that's the whole pitch. 🦀
blocks.body: Rust is a compiled, statically-typed systems programming language originally created by Graydon Hoare and later sponsored by Mozilla Research. Its headline feature is memory safety without a garbage collector: instead of cleaning up unused memory while your program runs, Rust's compiler enforces a strict set of ownership rules at compile time, catching entire categories of bugs — like using memory after it's been freed — before the program ever executes.

highlights.text: memory safety without a garbage collector

blocks.body: Rust is also a compiled language: the rustc compiler translates your source code directly into native machine code ahead of time, using the same LLVM backend that powers many C and C++ compilers. There's no interpreter reading your code line by line and no virtual machine running underneath it — just a standalone binary that runs on its own, which is a big part of why Rust programs tend to start instantly and run about as fast as C or C++.

blocks.sentence: Rust achieves memory ___ at compile time, without needing a garbage collector, through its ownership system.
blocks.explanation: Rust's ownership and borrowing rules are checked by the compiler before your program ever runs, ruling out whole classes of memory bugs without any runtime garbage collector.

blocks.robotComment: Zero-cost abstraction is a fancy way of saying: write it nicely, pay nothing for it. ⚙️
blocks.body: Rust is also statically typed, meaning every value's type is known and checked at compile time rather than discovered while the program runs. Combined with what the community calls zero-cost abstractions — high-level, convenient features that compile down to code just as fast as the equivalent hand-written low-level version — Rust lets you write expressive code without sacrificing the raw performance systems programmers care about.

blocks.question: What does it mean that Rust has 'zero-cost abstractions'?
options: High-level, convenient features compile down to code as fast as an equivalent hand-written low-level version
Rust itself is free and open source to download
Abstractions in Rust have no features at all
Rust programs never use any functions
blocks.explanation: Zero-cost abstractions means you don't pay a performance penalty for writing clean, high-level code — the compiler generates output just as efficient as if you'd written the low-level version by hand.

blocks.body: Rust has topped Stack Overflow's 'most loved programming language' survey for years running, but it's also known for a real learning curve: its ownership and borrow-checking rules feel unusual at first, even to experienced programmers coming from other languages. The payoff most people report is that once code compiles, it tends to just work — many bugs that would surface as crashes in other languages are caught by the compiler instead.

blocks.robotComment: 😄 Think about how Rust said it handles memory — no background cleanup process running.
blocks.statement: Rust manages memory using a garbage collector that runs in the background while the program executes, similar to Java.
blocks.explanation: Rust has no garbage collector. Memory is managed through ownership rules that the compiler checks before the program ever runs, so there's no runtime cleanup process at all.

blocks.robotComment: Rust spent years as one developer's side project before the world ever saw it. 🦀
blocks.body: Rust began in 2006 as a personal project by Graydon Hoare, a Mozilla employee experimenting with safer ways to write low-level software. Mozilla officially started sponsoring the project in 2009, and Rust was announced publicly for the first time in 2010, giving outside developers their first real look at it.

In its early years, the rustc compiler was itself written in OCaml. Around 2011, the team rewrote the compiler in Rust itself — a milestone called self-hosting, where a language's own compiler is written in that same language. Reaching self-hosting is often treated as a rite of passage that shows a young language is mature enough to build real software with.

blocks.sentence: Rust's first stable release, version ___, arrived in May 2015 along with a promise of stability without stagnation.
blocks.explanation: Rust 1.0 shipped in May 2015. From that point on, the team committed to never breaking existing code across future releases — 'stability without stagnation.'

blocks.robotComment: Not the metal, the fungus — and yes, that's the actual reason. 🍄
blocks.body: The name 'Rust' is generally credited to rust fungi, a family of fungi noted for being extremely hardy and difficult to eradicate — a fitting namesake for a language obsessed with reliability. It's also a short, memorable word that pairs naturally with Cargo, Rust's package manager and build tool, named after the cargo a ship carries.

blocks.question: Why is the language named 'Rust'?
options: It's named after rust fungi, a family of unusually hardy fungi, fitting its focus on reliability
It's named after creator Graydon Hoare's hometown
It's an acronym describing the compiler's internal architecture
It's named after the reddish color of its original logo
blocks.explanation: The name references rust fungi, chosen for their reputation as extremely hardy and hard to kill — a fitting theme for a language built around reliability.

blocks.body: Rust's development is now guided by editions — Rust 2015, 2018, 2021, and 2024 — which let the language add new features and even change some syntax rules without breaking code written for an older edition. In 2021, the independent Rust Foundation was created to steward the language's future, with founding corporate members including AWS, Google, Huawei, Microsoft, and Mozilla, after Mozilla scaled back its own involvement in the project.

blocks.statement: The Rust Foundation was created in 2021 to help govern the language's future after Mozilla scaled back its involvement.
blocks.explanation: The Rust Foundation launched in 2021 with founding members including AWS, Google, Huawei, Microsoft, and Mozilla, taking over stewardship of the project.

blocks.robotComment: When a bug at this level can crash an entire operating system, Rust's guarantees really start to matter. 🛡️
blocks.body: Rust has become a serious option for systems-level programming, the kind of work traditionally reserved for C and C++. Parts of the Linux kernel now accept Rust code alongside its long-standing C codebase, and Redox is an entire operating system, including its kernel, written in Rust from the ground up.

Rust is also a favorite for building fast command-line tools. ripgrep, a blazing-fast text search tool, is written in Rust and is bundled inside popular editors like VS Code to power their search-everywhere features. Similar Rust-built tools like fd (a faster find) and bat (a nicer cat) have become popular replacements for decades-old Unix utilities.

blocks.question: Which of these is a popular command-line search tool written in Rust?
blocks.explanation: ripgrep is a fast, Rust-built alternative to grep, and it powers the search feature inside several popular code editors.

blocks.body: Rust also compiles cleanly to WebAssembly (Wasm), a portable, near-native format that runs inside web browsers. That lets developers write performance-critical pieces of a web app — image processing, physics, games — in Rust, and run them alongside JavaScript at speeds JavaScript alone often can't match.

blocks.robotComment: Notice a pattern here — a lot of these are 'this absolutely cannot go down' kinds of systems. 🔒
blocks.body: On the backend, Discord rewrote several of its most latency-sensitive services in Rust, Dropbox uses it for parts of its file-storage infrastructure, and Amazon built Firecracker — the lightweight virtual machine technology behind AWS Lambda — entirely in Rust. Rust also underpins major blockchain projects like Solana, and the Bevy game engine is built with it too.

blocks.sentence: Amazon built ___, the lightweight virtual machine technology behind AWS Lambda, using Rust.
blocks.explanation: Firecracker is a Rust-built virtualization technology that AWS uses to run Lambda functions and other serverless workloads securely and efficiently.

blocks.statement: Rust cannot be compiled to WebAssembly, so it isn't used for browser-based applications.
blocks.explanation: Rust actually has excellent WebAssembly support, and compiling Rust to Wasm is a common way to run performance-critical code inside a web browser.

lessons.title: Setting Up a Project with Cargo

blocks.robotComment: One command, and Rust hands you a ready-to-run project — no folder-wrangling required. 📦
blocks.body: Cargo is Rust's built-in build tool and package manager — think of it as npm and a build system rolled into one, and it comes installed automatically alongside the Rust compiler. Running cargo new my_project creates a brand-new folder called my_project, already set up with everything a Rust project needs to compile and run.

code.caption: Creating a new Rust project called my_project, then moving into its folder.

blocks.body: That command creates two important things: a Cargo.toml file at the top level, and a src folder containing main.rs. Cargo.toml is the project's manifest — it lists the package's name, version, the Rust edition it targets, and any external dependencies it needs. src/main.rs is where your actual program code lives, and Cargo starts it off with a working 'Hello, world!' program already written for you.

code.caption: A freshly generated Cargo.toml — the project's manifest, with no dependencies added yet.

blocks.sentence: Cargo's project manifest, listing a package's name, version, and dependencies, is called ___.
blocks.explanation: Cargo.toml is the manifest file Cargo generates for every new project, holding its metadata and dependency list.

blocks.question: What does running cargo new my_project create?
options: A new project folder with a Cargo.toml manifest and a src/main.rs file already containing a working program
Only a single empty .rs file with no other setup
A compiled binary ready to distribute
A folder containing just documentation, with no code
blocks.explanation: cargo new scaffolds a complete, ready-to-build project: the Cargo.toml manifest plus a src/main.rs file with a starter "Hello, world!" program.

blocks.robotComment: Every Rust program needs exactly this one entry point — nothing runs without it. 🚪
blocks.body: Every runnable Rust program needs a function named main — it's the entry point the compiled program starts executing from. You declare it with the fn keyword, followed by the name, a pair of parentheses for its parameters, and a pair of curly braces holding the body.

code.caption: A complete Rust program. Execution starts at the top of main and runs each statement in order.

blocks.body: Rust uses curly braces {} to mark the body of a function, the same style used by C, Java, and JavaScript — unlike Python, which uses indentation alone. Each statement inside the body ends with a semicolon, and the compiler will refuse to build your program if you forget one on a statement that needs it.

blocks.robotComment: 😄 Think about what happens if rustc can't find a starting point.
blocks.statement: A Rust program will fail to compile if it has no fn main() function defined anywhere.
blocks.explanation: rustc needs a main function to know where execution should begin. Without one, the compiler reports an error instead of producing a runnable program.

blocks.question: In the program below, where does execution begin?

code.caption: The same complete Rust program shown above.

options: At the opening brace of fn main()
At the top of the file, regardless of what functions exist
At whichever function is defined last
Rust programs have no fixed starting point
blocks.explanation: Execution always begins inside fn main() — Rust looks specifically for a function named main to use as the entry point.

questions.question: What does cargo new my_project create?
options: A new project folder with a Cargo.toml manifest and a starter src/main.rs
A folder with documentation but no code

questions.sentence: Rust programs are declared as functions using the ___ keyword.

blocks.robotComment: That exclamation point isn't decoration — it's telling you something real. ❗
blocks.body: println! prints text to the screen, followed by a newline. Notice the exclamation point at the end of its name: that ! means println! is a macro, not an ordinary function. Macros are expanded into other code at compile time, which is how println! can safely check that your format string matches the values you passed it before the program even runs — a plain function couldn't do that.

code.caption: println! prints the text and moves to a new line automatically.

blocks.body: You can insert values into the printed text using curly-brace placeholders: {}. Each {} in the format string is filled in, in order, by the extra arguments you pass after it, separated by commas.

code.caption: Each {} placeholder is replaced by the matching argument, in the order they appear.

blocks.sentence: The ! at the end of println! signals that it's a ___ rather than an ordinary function.
blocks.explanation: The trailing ! marks println! (and Rust macros in general) as being expanded into other code at compile time, unlike a regular function call.

blocks.body: Rust also has print!, which works exactly like println! but doesn't add a trailing newline, so the next thing printed continues on the same line. There's also format!, which builds and returns a String instead of printing anything — handy when you want the formatted text for later instead of showing it right away.

blocks.question: What does println!("{} scored {}", "Sam", 90) print?

code.caption: A println! call with two placeholders and two arguments.

options: An error, since the arguments have different types
blocks.explanation: Each {} placeholder is filled in order by the matching argument — the first {} becomes "Sam" and the second becomes 90.

blocks.robotComment: The compiler skips right over these — they're purely for the humans reading the code. 📝
blocks.body: A comment is text in your source code that the Rust compiler completely ignores — it exists purely to explain something to a human reading the code later, including future you. In Rust, // starts a line comment: everything from // to the end of that line is ignored.

code.code:
// This calculates a 20% tip
let tip = bill * 0.2;
code.caption: A line comment explaining the purpose of the line below it.

blocks.body: For longer explanations, Rust also supports block comments with /* and */, which can span multiple lines and don't need to be repeated on every line the way // does.

code.caption: A block comment spanning several lines, placed above the code it describes.

blocks.sentence: A block comment in Rust starts with ___ and can span multiple lines.
blocks.explanation: Block comments start with /* and end with */, and unlike // comments, they can span as many lines as needed without repeating the symbol.

blocks.robotComment: 😄 Remember what a comment's whole job is.
blocks.statement: Comments in Rust can change how a program behaves when it runs.
blocks.explanation: Comments are stripped out before compilation even begins — they have no effect on the compiled program whatsoever.

blocks.question: Which symbol starts a single-line comment in Rust?
blocks.explanation: A double slash // starts a line comment in Rust, and everything after it on that line is ignored by the compiler.

blocks.robotComment: Same underlying compile step, two different jobs — knowing which one to reach for saves time. ⚙️
blocks.body: cargo build compiles your project into a runnable binary, but it doesn't run that binary for you — it just leaves it sitting in the target/debug folder, waiting. cargo run does both steps in one: it compiles the project (recompiling only if something changed since last time) and then immediately runs the resulting binary.

code.code:
cargo build
./target/debug/my_project

# vs. doing both in one step:
cargo run
code.caption: cargo build only compiles; you have to run the binary yourself. cargo run compiles and runs it for you.

blocks.body: There's also cargo check, which is faster than either: it asks the compiler to verify your code is correct without actually producing a runnable binary at all. It's handy while you're still writing code and just want quick feedback on whether it compiles.

blocks.sentence: Running ___ compiles a Rust project and then immediately runs the resulting binary, all in one step.
blocks.explanation: cargo run compiles the project (if needed) and runs it immediately, which is why it is the most common command during day-to-day development.

blocks.robotComment: Debug builds are for you; release builds are for everyone else. 🚀
blocks.body: By default, both cargo build and cargo run produce a debug build: fast to compile, but not very optimized, and placed in target/debug. Adding the --release flag, as in cargo build --release, produces a much more optimized binary in target/release — it takes noticeably longer to compile, but the resulting program runs significantly faster, which is what you'd ship to real users.

code.caption: Building an optimized release binary and running it directly from target/release.

blocks.robotComment: 😄 Think about which folder an unoptimized build lands in.
blocks.statement: Running cargo build without any flags produces an optimized binary in target/release.
blocks.explanation: Without --release, cargo build produces an unoptimized debug binary in target/debug. The optimized release binary only appears in target/release when you pass --release.
